stories.title: Vance says the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms, and Trump largely agrees
stories.summary: Vance blamed the war for the Republican rout, Trump called that 'largely true' but said he would do it again, and conservative writers split on the cause.
story: Vice President JD Vance wrote that "The reason we lost is the war," adding that "many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026." Fox News and the Washington Examiner reported his post. His fixes were to end the war, focus on cost of living, put America First and change the relationship with Israel. Asked about it, Trump told reporters the claim was "largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term" (The Hill, NBC News). He still defended the decision: "If I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again."

On election night Trump had said "I don't think it's the war, Bret, I think it's the gasoline price" (Fox News). Democrats now hold the House and, by NBC's projection, the Senate. CNN framed Vance's post as an attempt to protect his 2028 hopes by separating himself from Trump, while Fox reported he is courting disaffected Trump voters. Vance has said he has not decided whether to run.

Conservative commentators disagree on the cause. Ari Fleischer argued "The problem was not the Iran War. It was the cease fire" (Fox News). The Washington Examiner ran pieces blaming affordability, tariffs and weak candidates, and National Review argued Trump's tariffs hurt Republicans before the war began. Sen. Ted Cruz said the party did not focus enough on cost of living.
The argument matters because it sets the party's direction before 2028 and shapes the pressure on Trump over Iran, where a naval blockade continues.
stories.flag: Whether Vance's post was aimed at Trump or at the war itself is analysis from CNN, not something Vance stated.
facts: Vance posted that the war was the reason Republicans lost, reported by Fox News and the Washington Examiner.
Trump called the claim 'largely true' because the war pushed up gasoline prices, while saying he would do it again.
Trump said on election night that gasoline prices, not the war, were the issue.
Ari Fleischer blamed the ceasefire instead of the war, per Fox News.
Sen. Ted Cruz said Republicans did not focus enough on cost of living, per the Washington Examiner.
stories.left: The war was a choice Trump made without Congress, and voters punished it at the pump and at the ballot box. Vance's own admission shows even the administration sees the link. Democrats say Republicans who backed an unauthorized war and tariffs that raised prices should not be surprised by the result. The fix is to end the war, restore congressional authority and lower costs, not to rebrand the same agenda.
stories.right: Conservatives are right to argue about the cause instead of papering it over. Some, like Fleischer, say the failure was an unfinished war and a weak ceasefire, not the decision to confront Iran. Others, writing in National Review and the Examiner, say affordability and tariffs sank candidates before the first shot. A party that wants to win in 2028 has to fix the cost of living and explain its foreign policy in plain terms.
stories.next: Watch whether Trump changes course on Iran, and how Republicans handle Hegseth when the House returns Nov. 9.

stories.title: Mississippi Senate race stays too close to call with no recount process
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom leads Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by a margin that reports put between dozens and about 2,000 votes, and both parties prepare for court.
story: The Mississippi Senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith was still uncalled Thursday. Reported margins vary by time of report. NPR's early Wednesday count had Colom ahead by 43 votes, NBC cited fewer than 65 votes with more than 95% counted, and The Hill, citing Decision Desk HQ, put his lead at just under 2,000 votes on Thursday. NBC projects Democrats at 54 Senate seats to Republicans' 44, a net gain of seven.

Mississippi has no automatic recount and no mechanism for a candidate to request one, NPR and The Hill reported. A losing candidate would have to persuade a judge. On Thursday the NRSC and Hyde-Smith's lawyers asked election commissioners in all 82 counties to separate and preserve affidavit ballots (The Hill). Colom's campaign called it a "desperate stunt."

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Elias Law Group have sent staff to the state. The Mississippi GOP chair said the party will accept a Colom win if it happens, while saying he expects Hyde-Smith to be reelected if outstanding ballots are counted under the law. County officials must send results to the secretary of state by Nov. 13.
Alaska is also unresolved. NBC reported Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Sen. Dan Sullivan by 637 votes with 70% of ballots counted. The seat count could change.
stories.flag: Margins differ across NPR, NBC and The Hill because they were reported at different times. NBC's 54-seat figure may or may not include Mississippi and Alaska.
stories.blindspot: No right-leaning outlet coverage found; Republican positions come through The Hill and NBC reporting.
facts: NBC News projects Democrats win the Senate, 54 to 44.
Mississippi has no recount mechanism, per NPR and The Hill.
The NRSC asked all 82 counties to preserve affidavit ballots, per The Hill.
County results are due to the secretary of state by Nov. 13.
Alaska's Peltola led Sullivan by 637 votes with 70% counted, per NBC.
stories.left: Every legally cast ballot should be counted, and a race this close should be decided by the count, not by pre-emptive legal moves. Democrats say the preservation letter signals an effort to throw out affidavit ballots after the fact. They argue a state with no recount rule needs courts to protect the vote, and that a Colom win would add to a mandate for oversight.
stories.right: Republicans argue that provisional and affidavit ballots carry the highest risk of error and should be set aside and checked before they count. Asking officials to preserve them is a routine step in a razor-thin race, not a stunt. The state GOP's pledge to accept a Colom win if the law is followed shows the aim is a clean count, and the party can point to that as the standard.
stories.next: Watch the Nov. 13 certification deadline and any filing over affidavit ballots.

stories.title: Massie sets up a Hegseth impeachment vote as Republicans blame him for the rout
stories.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie says he will force a vote when the House returns, and Sen. Thom Tillis says Hegseth faces a reckoning.
story: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) plans to force a House vote to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth when Congress returns next week, with the House reported back Nov. 9, CNN and The Hill reported. CNN said several GOP sources expect it to pass. Massie gave Hegseth an ultimatum to resign or face impeachment, the Washington Examiner reported.

Massie introduced eight articles in September and four of them concern Hegseth's conduct of the Iran war, which Massie says is illegal because Congress never authorized it. Speaker Mike Johnson sent the House home early in September, and Massie and Democrats said that avoided a vote. Johnson called the push "a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention" (The Hill).

After Tuesday's losses, many Republicans are blaming Hegseth, CNN reported. Sen. Thom Tillis said he faces "a reckoning" in the lame-duck session (The Hill). Impeachment needs a simple House majority and Rep. Don Bacon is leaning against, per CNN. Trump has defended Hegseth. Removal would still need a Senate trial.
Democrats take over committees in January, and Armed Services' Adam Smith has said he wants to examine Hegseth's management of the Pentagon (ABC News).
facts: Massie introduced eight impeachment articles in September, four tied to the Iran war.
The House is reported to return Nov. 9.
Impeachment requires a simple majority in the House.
Rep. Don Bacon is leaning against, per CNN.
Trump has defended Hegseth.
stories.left: Hegseth ran a war that Congress never authorized, and voters have now said so. Democrats say impeachment is the constitutional remedy and that Republicans who suddenly care are reacting to polling, not principle. They want hearings on the war, boat strikes and the management of the Pentagon.
stories.right: Conservatives who oppose this say a lame-duck impeachment over a policy dispute sets a poor precedent and turns a disagreement about war powers into a partisan weapon. Others on the right, including Massie, say the war needed congressional approval and Hegseth should answer for it. The argument is whether election losses justify removing an official.
stories.next: Watch for the House vote after it returns Nov. 9.

stories.title: Democrats plan oversight blitz and Trump promises vetoes
stories.summary: Incoming committee chairs target Trump family business, immigration enforcement and the Iran war, while Trump says he will become 'Mr. Veto'.
story: Democrats won the House and, by NBC's projection, the Senate, and incoming committee chairs have started naming targets. Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely Oversight chair, listed the Trump family's businesses, immigration enforcement, corporate donations to the White House ballroom and the Epstein files (CNN). Jamie Raskin plans to look at how DOJ and the FBI treated Trump's opponents, and at pardons (ABC News).

Armed Services' Adam Smith wants to examine the Iran war, boat strikes and Hegseth's management (ABC News). The Hill reported that officials from Cabinet secretaries down to mid-level staff have hired lawyers. Sen. Ron Wyden posted a single word: "Subpoenas."

On legislation, Hakeem Jeffries named reversing Medicaid cuts, extending ACA credits, restoring congressional authority over tariffs and stopping the Iran war (NBC News). Trump said he would be "Mr. Veto" and added that "at some point we'll probably make deals" (NPR). Overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers. Democrats do not have that.
Analysts told NPR the affordability agenda may serve mainly as 2028 messaging unless Republicans cross over.
facts: Democrats take committee gavels in January, per ABC News.
Garcia named four Oversight targets, per CNN.
Jeffries' priorities include Medicaid cuts, ACA credits, tariffs and Iran, per NBC News.
Trump said he will use his veto power.
A veto override needs two-thirds of both chambers.
stories.left: Voters gave Democrats the power to check a president who has pushed far past normal limits, and oversight is the job. Democrats say they will also pass popular bills on health costs and tariffs, forcing Trump to veto measures that most Americans support. Investigations of family business dealings and the war are legitimate oversight, not retribution.
stories.right: Republicans warn that an oversight blitz will become a show of subpoenas and impeachments that distracts from cost of living, which was the voters' top concern. Trump's veto promise, they say, is a check on bills that fund spending increases or tie the president's hands on foreign policy. The party argues divided government should produce deals, not two years of investigations.
stories.next: Watch for committee assignments and the first subpoena threats when the new Congress is seated in January.

stories.title: Prop 40 billionaire tax appears headed for defeat while Prop 42 leads, and Becerra wins governor
stories.summary: Early returns have Prop 40 near 55% no and Prop 42 ahead, and Xavier Becerra will succeed Newsom.
story: California's Proposition 40 billionaire tax trailed with about 55% voting no and 60% of votes counted, CalMatters and the SF Chronicle reported, and the union behind it, SEIU-UHW, appeared to concede and said it would try again in 2028. Prop 42, which would ban any new wealth tax, led with 54%. If Prop 42 or Prop 41 gets more votes than Prop 40, it cancels the tax (CalMatters).

CalMatters reported Prop 42's main backer was Sergey Brin's group and that billionaires put in $159 million. Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed the tax and endorsed Prop 42. Prop 41, which targets the spending-limit workaround Prop 40 relies on, was trailing with 52% voting no.

Democrat Xavier Becerra won the governor's race and takes office in January, CalMatters and KQED reported. Republican Steve Hilton had about 34% in early counts. Becerra must submit a budget within days of taking office and inherits a deficit, CalMatters said. He has said he will keep many of Newsom's housing and mental health programs.

For the Bay Area, KQED and the SF Chronicle reported the regional transit tax passed, as covered in earlier editions. The SF Chronicle also showed Aisha Wahab leading Melissa Hernandez 56.5% to 43.4% in the District 14 congressional race with about half of ballots counted.
stories.flag: Prop 42's status is a projection. Counts are incomplete and CalMatters described it as both leading and passed.
stories.blindspot: No right-leaning outlet coverage found for this story in searches.
facts: Prop 40 trailed about 55% to 44% in early returns.
Prop 42 led with 54% at roughly 60% counted.
Brin's group was the main backer of Prop 42, with $159 million from billionaires, per CalMatters.
Becerra takes office in January after beating Steve Hilton.
Wahab led Hernandez 56.5% to 43.4% in District 14 early on Nov. 4.
stories.left: Supporters argued that billionaires pay a lower effective tax rate than workers and that California needs revenue to backfill federal health care cuts. They say $159 million of billionaire money shows how much the rich fear the idea, and that the losing margin does not mean voters like the status quo. The union says it will return in 2028.
stories.right: Opponents argue a wealth tax drives out the people who pay a large share of California's income tax and would hurt a state already facing a deficit. Prop 42's wide lead, backed by Newsom, suggests voters did not want to risk it. They also say the broader answer is to control spending, not to hunt for another revenue source.
stories.next: Watch the final counts as ballots are tallied, and Becerra's first budget in January.

stories.title: Newsom commutes all 548 California death sentences
stories.summary: The governor will convert every death sentence to life without parole, and about half of the cases need California Supreme Court review.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday that he will commute all 548 California death sentences to life without parole, CalMatters, the SF Chronicle, KQED and Fox News reported. He wrote that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, acknowledged the move does not repeal the death penalty, and said "These offenders will die in prison but not by our hand."

More than half of the cases, those involving people convicted of more than one felony, require review by the California Supreme Court under the state constitution (CalMatters). Becerra, the governor-elect, has committed to keeping the execution moratorium in place but has not said whether he will go further.

Prison reform groups celebrated. Michael Romano of Stanford's Three Strikes Project called it "the loudest and most important declaration that has been made in modern American history." Marc Klaas, whose daughter Polly was murdered, said "He just gave the gift of life to [hundreds of] people who took the gift of life from their victims." San Luis Obispo DA Dan Dow called the order an insult to murder victims (Fox News, SF Chronicle).
The timing comes as Newsom openly explores a presidential run, per coverage from the SF Chronicle and CalMatters.
facts: The order covers 548 death sentences.
Newsom said it does not repeal the death penalty.
More than half the cases need California Supreme Court review.
The decision comes during the lame-duck stretch before Becerra takes office in January.
Newsom is exploring a presidential run, per the SF Chronicle.
stories.left: Progressives say the death penalty is unreliable, racially uneven and costly, and a governor with clemency power should use it. They add that the sentence still keeps these prisoners behind bars for life, which Newsom said means they will die in prison.
stories.right: Critics say a governor is overriding juries, judges and appeals courts for these cases, and many voters backed the death penalty. They argue victims' families are being told their cases do not count and that the move looks timed to a presidential run. Supporters of capital punishment say that if Californians want change, they should vote on it.
stories.next: Watch for California Supreme Court review of the multi-felony cases and any lawsuits from prosecutors.

stories.title: IRGC says tankers burned in Hormuz as Trump weighs deal or force
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard blamed unauthorized routes for fires on two tankers and a tug, while Trump threatens to 'finish the job' without a nuclear deal.
story: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Thursday that two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz after trying unauthorized routes, and that one hit a mine, Fox News reported. The IRGC account is the only one found, and Fox did not independently verify the mine claim. CENTCOM called an Iranian claim about the blockade "false" and said the U.S. footprint remains intact.

Trump said he could "finish the job very easily" if Iran does not agree to a binding deal preventing a nuclear weapon (Fox News). Axios reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other advisers want the naval blockade and economic pressure to play out longer, and that there is no tidy way to finish the job.

After the midterms, NPR reported Iran is wary of new U.S. attacks, and Fox News reported Iranian leaders have presented the Republican losses as an anti-war rebuke. The IRGC has threatened U.S. bases if commercial ships keep transiting the strait, and Netanyahu has said Israel would join any renewed campaign (Axios).
WTI crude closed at $91.39, up 0.96%, per Yahoo Finance data. Oil has fallen in recent weeks from above $100.
stories.flag: The mine claim comes only from the IRGC. Reports that Tehran sent a formal nuclear proposal through Qatar appeared in a roundup and were not independently confirmed.
facts: The IRGC said two tankers and a tug burned after using unauthorized routes.
CENTCOM called an Iranian claim about the blockade false.
Trump said he could 'finish the job very easily' without a binding deal.
Axios reported advisers want the blockade to run longer.
WTI crude closed at $91.39.
stories.left: The war has no authorization from Congress, no end in sight and has cost Republicans an election. Progressives say the Hormuz incidents show the risk of open-ended escalation and that Trump's threats paint him into a corner. They want a diplomatic path, congressional votes and oversight of Hegseth.
stories.right: Conservatives who back the war say Iran has fired on shipping, laid mines and stalled on nuclear talks, so pressure is the only language Tehran respects. They argue an early exit would reward the IRGC, and that the blockade is a cheaper tool than a new strike. Some on the right, like Vance, argue the war should end for political and strategic reasons.
stories.next: Watch for any Iranian nuclear proposal, Trump's response, and shipping data through the strait.

stories.title: October jobs report lands Friday after a selloff that cooled Fed hike odds
stories.summary: Forecasts call for 59,000 to 65,000 jobs, and odds of a December Fed hike fell from about 83% to 66%.
story: The October jobs report comes out Friday at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, CNBC reported. The Dow Jones consensus is a gain of 59,000 jobs, up from 29,000 in September, and FactSet's consensus is 65,000. Unemployment is expected to hold at 4.2% and average hourly earnings to rise 0.3%.

The Fed raised rates a quarter point in September to 3.75% to 4%, its first hike since 2023, CNBC reported. Markets had priced a December hike, but odds on the CME FedWatch tool fell from about 83% to 66% on Thursday as stocks fell. The next meeting is Dec. 9. A CNBC headline said Fed official Barkin sees hikes ahead at a gradual pace.

The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.84%, per Yahoo Finance data, as traders left tech stocks (CNBC). Bloomberg reported Treasuries rallied earlier this week as oil fell, easing worries about more hikes. Oil rose Thursday.
Officials raised 2026 inflation forecasts to 3.7% for headline PCE and 3.4% for core in September (CNBC).
stories.blindspot: No right-leaning outlet coverage found for this story in searches.
stories.flag: The Barkin headline was seen in search results only, and his remarks were not read.
facts: Dow Jones consensus is 59,000 jobs and FactSet is 65,000.
September payrolls were 29,000.
Unemployment is forecast at 4.2%.
December hike odds fell from about 83% to 66%, per CME FedWatch.
The 10-year yield closed at 4.84%.
stories.left: A job market adding fewer than 100,000 jobs a month with rate hikes on top shows the economy is being squeezed by tariffs, war-driven energy costs and a Fed tightening into weakness. Progressives argue further hikes would hit working families hardest and that Congress should act on prices and health costs instead.
stories.right: Conservatives argue the Fed must keep fighting inflation, which remains well above target at 3.4% core PCE, and that war and tariff shocks are a policy issue for the White House. Many also say regulation and the cost of energy hold back hiring, and that growth depends on lower costs, not rate relief.
stories.next: Friday 8:30 a.m. ET jobs report, then the Fed meeting Dec. 9.

stories.title: Nasdaq falls 5.52% into correction as AI and chip stocks collapse
stories.summary: Nvidia lost 9.26% and the Magnificent 7 shed more than $1 trillion after midterm results raised fears of a slower data center buildout.
story: The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315.00 on Thursday, its worst day since April 2025, and entered correction territory. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36% to 7,353.73 and the Dow fell 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to 51,523.06 (Fox Business, CNBC, Yahoo Finance data). CNBC said the Magnificent 7 lost more than $1 trillion in market value, with Nvidia down 9.26% and losing more than $440 billion.

The tech sector had its worst day since March 2020, with the XLK fund down 8.04%, CNBC reported. Axios and CNBC tied the move to fears that Democrats' midterm wins and Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's promised data center moratorium will slow AI buildout. Qualcomm also fell after a weak earnings forecast. A higher oil price added pressure.

Analysts disagree on how far it will go. Altimeter's Brad Gerstner warned 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI capacity may not come online in 2027, while Dan Ives estimated about 10% of planned U.S. data centers could be scrapped (CNBC). Others said the reaction went too far, and one noted the Nasdaq has historically gained an average of 9.41% over three months after a correction low.
The turn was sharp. On Wednesday the Dow gained 3.03% and Big Tech surged on hopes of gridlock, then reversed Thursday.
stories.flag: Nvidia's drop is cited as 8% to 9.26% in different reports. This edition uses the Yahoo Finance close of 9.26%.
facts: Nasdaq closed at 24,315.00, down 5.52%.
S&P 500 closed at 7,353.73, down 4.36%.
Dow closed at 51,523.06, down 3.44%.
Nvidia fell 9.26% to $181.60; Microsoft fell 3.58%.
The Magnificent 7 lost more than $1 trillion, per CNBC.
stories.why: The AI trade now carries political risk as well as financing risk. Texas holds a large share of planned data center capacity, so a moratorium would hit chip demand, power equipment and the neocloud lenders.
stories.next: Jobs report Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET, then Nvidia earnings Nov. 17 after the close.

stories.title: Tesla falls 10.77% and Musk's companies lose over $420 billion after the midterms
stories.summary: Investors fear congressional probes and tougher regulation of Musk's businesses, and Tesla is down about 24% this year.
story: Tesla fell 10.77% to $343.69 on Thursday, following a 3.3% drop Wednesday, Bloomberg and Fox Business reported. CNBC said Tesla and SpaceX together lost over $420 billion in market value after the midterms. Bloomberg put Tesla's decline for the year at about 24%.

CNBC said investors worry that Democratic committee chairs will open probes of Musk's companies, and that regulatory scrutiny could block a Musk push to merge SpaceX and Tesla. Deutsche Bank, cited by CNBC, said SpaceX's Texas compute capacity could face delays after Hinojosa's win.
The pressure on Musk stocks began Wednesday. Bloomberg reported his stocks erased $130 billion early as Texas turned blue, while Big Tech surged.
Tesla is on Keanu's watchlist. The broader AI trade fell on the same day, so the Musk-specific part of the move is unclear.
stories.flag: How much of the drop is Musk-specific and how much reflects the market-wide AI selloff is not established.
facts: Tesla closed at $343.69, down 10.77%.
Tesla fell 3.3% on Wednesday, per Bloomberg.
Tesla and SpaceX lost over $420 billion combined, per CNBC.
Tesla is down about 24% for the year, per Bloomberg.
Deutsche Bank flagged SpaceX's Texas compute capacity as at risk.
stories.why: Musk's businesses depend on federal contracts and permissions and on Texas power and land. A Democratic Congress and Texas governor raise regulatory risk for Tesla, SpaceX and xAI at once.
stories.next: Watch for House Oversight and Commerce letters to Musk's companies once Democrats take committees in January.

stories.title: Texas grid faces 474 gigawatts of data center requests as the buildout hits politics
stories.summary: ERCOT is auditing hundreds of proposals by Dec. 10, and 800 VDC designs are still under review.
story: ERCOT is tracking 474 gigawatts of new connection requests, about 90% of them data centers, which is more than five times the grid's total peak demand, according to IEEE Spectrum, Axios and TechCrunch reporting. ERCOT plans to audit hundreds of data center proposals by Dec. 10 as part of Gov. Greg Abbott's pause on new interconnections.

MIT Technology Review reported that Democrats won the Texas governor's race and the Senate seat and will control the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. The Stargate Frontier site in Shackelford County is projected at 1,820 megawatts and a Dallas-area project at 6,400 megawatts. Whether projects already under construction are exempt from a Hinojosa moratorium has been reported as likely but is not settled.

On the engineering side, ERCOT's Large Load Working Group is still evaluating 800 VDC facility designs, and one analysis said Texas is far from ready for them (IEEE Spectrum). Nvidia expects 800 VDC facilities to start appearing in 2027. Converting medium-voltage AC straight to about 800 V DC at the site perimeter removes most intermediate conversion stages.
Batteries are one answer to load swings. IEEE Spectrum reported Dimaag's system aims to buffer fast AI load changes and ride through short voltage dips.
stories.flag: The date of Abbott's halt differs by source: TechCrunch and Axios place it in early August, while MIT Technology Review says September 21. Hinojosa's policy is not law and depends on the 2027 session.
facts: ERCOT's queue holds 474 GW of requests, about 90% data centers.
ERCOT plans to audit hundreds of proposals by Dec. 10.
Stargate Frontier is projected at 1,820 MW.
Nvidia expects 800 VDC data centers in 2027.
Hinojosa's moratorium is not yet law.
stories.why: Grid interconnection and power delivery, not chips, may set the pace of AI growth. If Texas slows approvals, developers will move capacity to other states or build off-grid with batteries and on-site generation.
stories.next: Dec. 10 is the ERCOT audit target, and the Texas legislature meets in 2027.

stories.title: Qualcomm's handset chip sales fall 26% as memory costs hit phone demand
stories.summary: Higher memory prices push phone makers to raise prices, and Qualcomm guided below expectations and fell more than 9% on Thursday.
story: Qualcomm reported handset chip revenue down 26% to $5.14 billion, slightly below the $5.21 billion estimate, CNBC reported Wednesday. It guided to adjusted EPS of $2.15 to $2.35 on $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion in revenue, below the $2.27 and $10.48 billion analysts expected. The stock fell about 7% and then more than 9% on Thursday.

The cause is memory. Rising memory costs are pushing handset makers to raise prices, which hurts demand (CNBC), a squeeze earlier editions tied to AI data centers. In July, Qualcomm's CEO said "Cost went up, prices are going to go up."

Management said handset sales are starting to recover sequentially and that Android shipments in China have bottomed, but expects the overall handset market to be flat in 2027. It expects $5 billion in data center revenue in fiscal 2027 and said in July it targets non-phone sales at 60% of revenue next year.
The squeeze links the two ends of the AI buildout: chips for data centers raise costs for consumer devices.
facts: Handset revenue was $5.14 billion, down 26%.
Guidance was $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion in revenue.
Qualcomm expects a flat handset market in 2027.
It targets $5 billion in data center revenue in fiscal 2027.
The stock fell more than 9% Thursday, per CNBC.
stories.why: Memory supply is now a limit on consumer hardware. Phone makers face higher bills of materials, and Qualcomm's shift to data center chips depends on the same AI spending that is under pressure.
stories.next: Watch Apple and Android makers' pricing and memory prices.

stories.title: SLAC X-ray laser makes the shortest high-energy pulses yet, at 100 to 400 attoseconds
stories.summary: A Nature Photonics paper measured 9 keV pulses lasting a few hundred attoseconds and confirmed the duration with a new diagnostic.
story: Researchers at SLAC's Linac Coherent Light Source measured X-ray pulses of about 9 kiloelectronvolts lasting 100 to 400 attoseconds, the shortest high-energy pulses ever recorded at an X-ray free-electron laser, according to Stanford News and Newswise. The work appeared in Nature Photonics on Oct. 20 (I. Inoue et al.). An attosecond is one quintillionth of a second.

Earlier claims of hard X-ray attosecond pulses were not directly verified. The team used a method in which intensely focused X-ray pulses excite an element and make it fluoresce in the forward direction, and the fluorescence carries information about the pulse's energy, shape and duration. Lead researcher Agostino Marinelli said making the pulses took several years but "measuring pulses this short is really, really difficult."
SLAC called it the first diagnostic that proves the pulses are only a few hundred attoseconds long. Earlier SLAC work in 2018 reported hard X-ray pulses of a few hundred attoseconds.
Pulses this short can capture electron motion inside molecules as chemical bonds form.
stories.flag: One search result gave 170 attoseconds as a duration, but SLAC and Newswise reported 100 to 400, so the range is used here.
facts: Pulses were about 9 keV and lasted 100 to 400 attoseconds.
The paper is by Inoue et al. in Nature Photonics, Oct. 20.
The method uses forward X-ray fluorescence from an element.
Lead researcher is Agostino Marinelli.
It is the first diagnostic confirming the duration, per SLAC.
stories.why: Measuring electron motion needs a probe shorter than the motion itself. Verified attosecond hard X-rays open direct views of charge flow in materials and molecules.
stories.next: Watch for first experiments that use the pulses on real samples.

stories.title: NASA-funded study dates Mars meteorite Teghaza 001 to over 4.1 billion years
stories.summary: The rock found in the Sahara in 2022 matches southern highlands minerals seen from orbit and is called one of the oldest Mars meteorites.
story: A NASA-funded study details Teghaza 001, a roughly 800-gram rose-colored meteorite found in the Sahara in 2022, NASA and JPL reported. Age dating of its minerals shows it comes from a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago. The lead author is Yang Liu of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Its mineralogy lines up with what NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter has seen in the cratered southern highlands. No one can say exactly where on Mars it came from, though the paper names several candidate locations. One reviewer called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars (NASA).

The 'oldest' label needs care. Space.com has described ALH84001 as dated to about 4.09 billion years and NWA 7034, 'Black Beauty', to about 4.5 billion years, and these figures come from different eras and methods. NASA's wording is 'one of the oldest'.
The announcement appeared about a week ago.
stories.flag: Whether Teghaza 001 is older than other Martian meteorites depends on the dating method, so NASA's 'one of the oldest' is used.
facts: Teghaza 001 weighs about 800 grams and was found in the Sahara in 2022.
Minerals show it formed more than 4.1 billion years ago.
Lead author is Yang Liu of JPL.
Its minerals match southern highlands seen by MRO.
Its exact origin on Mars is unknown.
stories.why: Old samples record the early crust and water history of Mars, a time when few samples exist on Earth. A lab-dated rock tied to orbital maps helps calibrate what rovers and orbiters see.
stories.next: Watch for the Mars Sample Return decisions and further analyses of the rock.

stories.title: Sanders and other Democrats call for a national data center moratorium, but leadership splits
stories.summary: Sanders posted 'National data center moratorium now' while Schumer favors cost rules and Fetterman calls a pause 'lunacy'.
story: After the midterms Sen. Bernie Sanders posted "National data center moratorium now," CNBC reported. Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced a bill in March to bar new data centers until AI safeguards are enacted. Sen. Elizabeth Warren wants a moratorium until developers show they will cover full costs, and Rep. Frank Pallone supports a pause (The Hill).

Party leaders are divided. Chuck Schumer favors enforceable cost rules over a pause and called a pause bill a "toothless messaging bill" (The Hill). Hakeem Jeffries has said a pause is "certainly not a position" he has articulated. Sen. John Fetterman called it "lunacy."
Voters moved first. CNBC reported voters sided against data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures on Tuesday, and Texas elected Gina Hinojosa on a moratorium pledge.

Republicans are weighing in. The Hill carried an opinion piece arguing Democrats are threatening U.S. AI supremacy and that Republicans should pounce, and Senate Democrats earlier blocked a Republican Ratepayer Protection Act.
stories.flag: Some of The Hill's reporting on Democratic positions is older than this week, so positions may have shifted.
facts: Sanders posted 'National data center moratorium now' after the election.
Sanders and AOC introduced a moratorium bill in March.
Voters rejected data centers in 40 of 41 local measures, per CNBC.
Schumer prefers mandatory cost rules to a pause.
Fetterman called a pause 'lunacy'.
stories.left: Data centers raise power bills, strain water and grid supply, and arrive with tax breaks that benefit giant firms. Progressives say a pause until ratepayer protections and safeguards exist is a reasonable demand, and 40 of 41 local votes show where the public stands. Moderates counter with mandatory cost rules that keep construction going.
stories.right: Conservatives and many in the industry argue a moratorium would hand AI leadership to China, cost construction jobs and raise power-sector investment costs without lowering bills. The Hill's opinion writers say the right should defend building and offer its own ratepayer protections. They point to the market losing more than $1 trillion in megacap value in one day on fears of a slowdown.
stories.why: Data center policy is moving from local zoning fights to a national party platform. That affects chip demand, utility planning and who pays for new power plants.
stories.next: Watch for the first bills when the new Congress convenes in January and for Hinojosa's 2027 Texas agenda.

stories.title: Anthropic's IPO filing leaves valuation open as the AI trade sells off
stories.summary: The Oct. 26 S-1 lists the Nasdaq ticker ANT, a $965 billion last private valuation and an $80.75 billion first-half net loss.
story: Anthropic filed its public S-1 on Oct. 26, planning to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT," CNBC and Axios reported. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are lead underwriters, and shares could begin trading before Thanksgiving. The filing sets no price range.

Its last private round in May raised $65 billion at a $965 billion valuation. Press estimates for the IPO value vary widely, with one report at $1.5 trillion to over $2 trillion and another at $1 trillion to $2 trillion.

For the first half of 2026 Anthropic reported $16.29 billion in revenue and an $80.75 billion net loss, about $72 billion of which came from accounting charges tied to convertible notes. The Amodei siblings and five other co-founders will hold 50.1% of voting power through Founder LLC.
Disclosure: this edition is written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic. The facts here are as reported by CNBC and Axios.
stories.flag: Earlier editions reported a roadshow possibly starting the week of Nov. 9. That was not reconfirmed in today's searches, and no reporting found yet says whether the selloff changes the timing.
facts: The S-1 was filed Oct. 26 with ticker ANT on the Nasdaq.
The last private round raised $65 billion at $965 billion in May.
First-half revenue was $16.29 billion and net loss $80.75 billion.
About $72 billion of the loss was accounting charges on convertible notes.
Founders will hold 50.1% of voting power.
stories.why: Anthropic is the first big test of AI valuations in public markets. A sell-off of this size in chip and AI stocks may change the appetite for the offering, which some reports speculate could be around $100 billion.
stories.next: Watch for a price range filing and a roadshow date.
